main_claims: The proposed framework enables semi-automatic creation of linguistically challenging data-to-text corpora from existing Knowledge Bases, suitable for training wide-coverage micro-planners and KB verbalizers.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper presents a logically structured argument for a novel framework to create data-to-text corpora, specifically targeting the training of wide-coverage micro-planners. It begins by critiquing existing corpus creation methods, identifying gaps in supporting complex micro-planning tasks. The proposed framework, detailed in Section 3, aims to address these by leveraging real Knowledge Bases (DBpedia) and a multi-stage crowdsourcing process. The core of the argument lies in the comparative analysis (Section 4) of the newly created DBPNLG dataset against an existing benchmark (RNNLG). This comparison uses a range of data, text, and model performance metrics to demonstrate DBPNLG's superior diversity and complexity, thereby supporting the claims that it is more challenging for neural generators and better suited for micro-planning. The argument flow is generally coherent, moving from problem identification to solution proposal, detailed methodology, empirical validation, and concluding with implications for the field. However, some linkages between specific framework design choices and the measured micro-planning benefits could be more explicitly elaborated, and the interpretation of model performance as a direct measure of 'micro-planning complexity' could benefit from deeper linguistic analysis.
logical_argument_graph: Existing NLG corpora (domain-specific, expert-annotated, prior crowdsourced) are insufficient for training wide-coverage micro-planners due to limitations in scope, cost, or linguistic diversity (Section 1, Section 2).

A novel semi-automatic framework is proposed to create linguistically challenging data-to-text corpora from existing Knowledge Bases, specifically designed to support wide-coverage micro-planners and KB verbalizers (C1, Section 3).
The framework addresses shortcomings of prior crowdsourced methods by using 'real' KB data (DBpedia) and allowing for deeper input shapes, enabling training of KB verbalizers (C4, Section 3).

The framework's crowdsourcing methodology ensures a direct match between data and text, allowing a clear focus on micro-planning, and supports various micro-planning subtasks by matching data of increasing size with diverse texts (C5, C6, Section 3).

Applying this framework to DBpedia yields the DBPNLG dataset, which is empirically shown to be more diverse than the RNNLG dataset across multiple data and text characteristics (C2, Section 4.1, Section 4.2).

Specifically, DBPNLG has more diverse attributes, similar input patterns despite smaller size, a lower input/pattern ratio (reducing overfitting, increasing coverage), more diverse input shapes, longer texts, more sentences per text, higher text per input (for paraphrases), and greater lexical variety and sophistication (C7, C8, Section 4.1, Section 4.2).

Empirical evaluation using a sequence-to-sequence model demonstrates that DBPNLG presents a more complex and challenging learning task for neural generators, as evidenced by higher perplexity and lower BLEU scores compared to RNNLG (C3, Section 4.3).

Therefore, the proposed framework is a novel and effective method for creating challenging, diverse, and linguistically rich data-to-text corpora suitable for advancing research in wide-coverage micro-planning and KB verbalization (Section 5).

concerns.title: Ambiguity in 'Complexity' Interpretation for Micro-planning
concerns.description: The paper claims that lower BLEU and higher perplexity scores on DBPNLG indicate a 'more complex and challenging learning task' (C3). While plausible, the argument does not sufficiently elaborate on *how* these general NLG metrics specifically reflect the complexity of *micro-planning subtasks* (lexicalisation, aggregation, etc.) beyond general linguistic diversity. The link between model performance and specific micro-planning challenges could be more explicit and linguistically grounded.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper introduces a semi-automatic framework for constructing data-to-text corpora from Knowledge Bases, specifically designed to support the training of wide-coverage micro-planners. The methodology integrates a content selection module, adapted from prior work, to extract varied and coherent data units from DBpedia, with a multi-step crowdsourcing process for text generation and quality control. The framework's instantiation, the DBPNLG dataset, is then quantitatively compared against the RNNLG dataset across various data and text characteristics (e.g., attribute diversity, input patterns, lexical variety). To assess the learning task complexity, a sequence-to-sequence model's performance (perplexity, BLEU) is evaluated on both datasets. The central argument is that DBPNLG is more diverse and challenging, as evidenced by lower model performance, thereby making it more suitable for advanced micro-planning research.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript proposes a semi-automatic framework for creating linguistically challenging data-to-text corpora from existing Knowledge Bases, specifically targeting the training of wide-coverage micro-planners and KB verbalizers. It builds upon and refines existing crowdsourcing approaches to corpus creation, which the authors argue suffer from limitations such as reliance on artificial data and restricted input shapes (e.g., Wen et al., 2016). The core incremental contribution lies in combining a sophisticated content selection module (adapted from Perez-Beltrachini et al., 2016) to extract varied and coherent data units from real KBs (DBpedia) with a structured crowdsourcing process designed to ensure a direct data-text match and elicit linguistically diverse texts. The resulting DBPNLG dataset is empirically compared to the RNNLG dataset (Wen et al., 2016), demonstrating greater diversity in attributes, input patterns, and input shapes, as well as higher lexical variety and sophistication in the generated texts, despite being smaller in size. Furthermore, empirical evaluation using a sequence-to-sequence model shows lower performance (higher perplexity, lower BLEU) on DBPNLG, indicating that it presents a more complex and challenging learning task for neural generators. The paper thus incrementally advances the state-of-the-art in NLG corpus creation by providing a method to generate more realistic, diverse, and challenging benchmarks that are better suited for developing robust micro-planners.
logical_argument_graph: Existing NLG corpora (domain-specific, expert-annotated, prior crowdsourced) have limitations, particularly in supporting wide-coverage micro-planners and KB verbalizers (Section 1, Section 2).

Prior crowdsourced methods (e.g., Wen et al., 2016) use artificial data and limited input shapes (depth-one trees), which restricts linguistic coverage and the complexity of micro-planning operations that can be learned (Section 3).
The paper proposes a novel framework for semi-automatically creating data-to-text corpora from existing Knowledge Bases (e.g., DBpedia) to address these shortcomings (Claim C1, Section 3).
This framework integrates a content selection module (Perez-Beltrachini et al., 2016) to extract varied, relevant, and coherent data units from KBs (Assumption A4, Section 3.2).

It also includes a structured crowdsourcing process with quality checks to associate data units with human-authored texts, ensuring a direct data-text match and promoting linguistic diversity (Assumption A5, Section 3.3).
The resulting DBPNLG dataset, created from DBpedia, is more diverse than RNNLG in terms of attributes, input patterns, and input shapes (Claim C2, Section 4.1).
DBPNLG texts also exhibit higher lexical variety and sophistication, and a higher text-per-input ratio, providing a better basis for learning paraphrases (Claim C2, Claim C8, Section 4.2).

NLG models (sequence-to-sequence) trained on DBPNLG show lower performance (higher perplexity, lower BLEU) compared to RNNLG, indicating that DBPNLG presents a more complex and challenging learning task (Claim C3, Section 4.3).

Therefore, the proposed framework enables the semi-automatic creation of linguistically challenging data-to-text corpora from existing KBs, suitable for training wide-coverage micro-planners and KB verbalizers, incrementally improving upon existing methods (Claim C1, Claim C4, Claim C5, Claim C6, Section 5).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper addresses a critical gap in Natural Language Generation (NLG) research: the lack of suitable data-to-text corpora for training 'wide-coverage micro-planners' capable of handling complex linguistic phenomena like lexicalization, aggregation, and referring expression generation. It argues that existing corpora are either too domain-specific, costly to create (expert-annotated), or lack the necessary linguistic diversity and data-text fidelity (prior crowdsourced datasets using artificial data). To overcome this, the paper proposes a novel semi-automatic framework for creating such linguistically challenging corpora directly from existing Knowledge Bases (KBs). This framework integrates a sophisticated content selection module (derived from prior work on RDF content building) with a multi-stage, quality-controlled crowdsourcing process. The authors apply this framework to DBpedia, creating the DBPNLG dataset, and empirically demonstrate its superior diversity in terms of input characteristics (attributes, patterns, shapes) and text characteristics (lexical variety, sophistication, text per input) compared to a prominent existing benchmark (RNNLG). The paper further supports its claim of increased challenge by showing that a standard sequence-to-sequence NLG model performs significantly worse on DBPNLG, thereby positioning the framework and resulting dataset as a disruptive contribution to the field by providing a more realistic and demanding benchmark for future NLG model development.
logical_argument_graph: Existing data-to-text corpora are inadequate for training wide-coverage micro-planners due to limitations in domain specificity, cost of expert annotation, or insufficient linguistic complexity/data-text match in prior crowdsourced efforts.

This framework combines a content selection module (to extract varied, relevant, coherent data units from KBs like DBpedia) with a rigorous crowdsourcing process (ensuring direct data-text match and quality).

The DBPNLG dataset, created using this framework from DBpedia, exhibits significantly greater diversity in input characteristics (attributes, input patterns, input shapes) and text characteristics (length, lexical variety, sophistication, text per input) compared to the RNNLG dataset.

This increased diversity and complexity in DBPNLG makes it a more challenging learning task for neural NLG models, as evidenced by lower performance (higher perplexity, lower BLEU) of a sequence-to-sequence model trained on it compared to RNNLG.

Therefore, the proposed framework offers a novel method for generating challenging, linguistically rich datasets that can drive advancements in wide-coverage micro-planning and KB verbalization for NLG.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary:
The paper's central argument is that existing data-to-text corpora are insufficient for training wide-coverage micro-planners due to limitations in domain specificity, cost of expert annotation, or lack of linguistic diversity and data-text fidelity in prior crowdsourced datasets. To address this, the authors propose a novel semi-automatic framework that combines content selection from existing Knowledge Bases (specifically DBpedia) with a structured, quality-controlled crowdsourcing process. This framework is claimed to produce linguistically challenging corpora suitable for micro-planning and KB verbalization.

The core claims regarding the framework's novelty and its ability to generate diverse and complex datasets are largely supported by the detailed methodological description and the comparative empirical analysis. The framework's design, integrating a content selection module (adapted from Perez-Beltrachini et al., 2016) with a multi-step crowdsourcing protocol, is well-articulated and aims to overcome the identified shortcomings of previous approaches, particularly the use of artificial data and limited input shapes in datasets like RNNLG. The claims about DBPNLG's superior diversity in terms of attributes, input patterns, input shapes, lexical variety (CTTR), and sophistication (LS) compared to RNNLG are strongly supported by the quantitative statistics presented in Tables 3 and 4.

However, the claim that DBPNLG presents a 'more complex and challenging learning task for neural generators' based on lower performance (higher perplexity, lower BLEU) of a specific sequence-to-sequence model (Vinyals et al., 2015) is partially supported. While the empirical results for *that specific model* are clear, generalizing this to *all neural generators* or interpreting these metrics as a comprehensive measure of 'micro-planning complexity' for all NLG paradigms introduces an element of overstatement. The prior stage analyses also highlighted this as a key uncertainty. The framework's features for KB verbalizers and micro-planning subtasks are well-supported by its design rationale and the examples provided, demonstrating the *intent* and *potential* of the dataset for these specific applications. The implications of the input/pattern ratio and text-per-input ratio for learning and paraphrasing are logically derived from the observed quantitative differences.

Specifically, prior crowdsourced corpora (e.g., RNNLG) use artificial data and have limited input shapes, hindering KB verbalization and linguistic diversity (Section 3).
A novel semi-automatic framework is proposed to create linguistically challenging data-to-text corpora from existing KBs (e.g., DBpedia) (Section 3).
This framework combines a content selection module (Perez-Beltrachini et al., 2016) with a multi-step, quality-controlled crowdsourcing process (Section 3.2, 3.3).
The framework's design ensures suitability for KB verbalizers (using real KBs) and a clear focus on micro-planning (direct data-text match, varied data sizes for subtasks) (Section 3).
The DBPNLG dataset, created using this framework from DBpedia, is empirically compared to the RNNLG dataset (Section 4).

DBPNLG demonstrates greater diversity in data characteristics (attributes, input patterns, input shapes) and text characteristics (length, sentences, lexical variety, sophistication) compared to RNNLG (Section 4.1, 4.2).

The lower input/pattern ratio and higher text/input ratio in DBPNLG indicate a less repetitive dataset, harder learning, reduced overfitting risk, wider linguistic coverage, and better support for paraphrases (Section 4.1, 4.2).
A sequence-to-sequence model shows lower performance (higher perplexity, lower BLEU) on DBPNLG compared to RNNLG (Section 4.3).
This lower performance indicates that DBPNLG presents a more complex and challenging learning task for neural generators (Section 4.3).
Therefore, the proposed framework and the DBPNLG dataset offer a valuable resource for advancing research in wide-coverage NLG and micro-planning (Section 5).

- The assessment of DBPNLG's 'complexity' for neural generators relies on a single sequence-to-sequence model and standard metrics (BLEU, perplexity), which may not fully generalize to other NLG architectures or comprehensively capture the nuanced micro-planning challenges.

Introduction Concept-to-text generation broadly refers to the task of automatically producing textual output from non-linguistic input (Reiter & Dale, 2000). Depending on the application and the domain at hand, the input may assume various representations including databases of records, expert system knowl- edge bases, simulations of physical systems and so on. Figure 1 shows input examples and their corresponding text for three domains: air travel, sportscasting and weather forecast generation. A typical concept-to-text generation system implements a pipeline architecture consisting of three core stages, namely content planning (selecting the appropriate content from the input and determining the structure of the target text), sentence planning (determining the structure and lexi- cal content of individual sentences), and surface realization (rendering the speciﬁcation chosen by the sentence planner into a surface string). Traditionally, these components are hand-engineered in order to generate high quality text, at the expense of portability and scalability. It is thus no sur- prise that recent years have witnessed a growing interest in automatic methods for creating trainable generation components. Examples include learning which database records should be present in a text (Duboue & McKeown, 2002; Barzilay & Lapata, 2005) and how these should be verbalized (Liang, Jordan, & Klein, 2009).
